definition: Emend means to correct errors in a written text.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word emend. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know emend should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The choir director emended the hand-copied hymnal, restoring the sharps a careless copyist had dropped.
Proofreading stops short of emending — a proofreader hunts and marks the errors; emending actually sets the words right.
Rewrite goes further than emend — an emended paragraph keeps its author's words with the faults repaired; a rewritten one starts over from a blank line.

Correct is the everyday word for putting any mistake right — a sum, a posture, a spelling. Emend is its bookish cousin with a narrow home: you emend only written text, restoring what the words were meant to say. Every emendation corrects, but you cannot emend a golf swing.

Edit means to shape a text for length, clarity, or style, and an editor may cut or recast whole passages that contain no errors at all. Emend is narrower and humbler: it touches nothing but faults, repairing slips so the text finally reads as its author intended.

Grandma mends on Thursday evenings, with the radio on.
Emend means to correct errors in a written text.
Before the menus went out, the owner emended the printer's proof by hand: the 'sea brass' became sea bass again, and the fifteen-dollar soup returned to five.
Emend is correction with a scholar's precision — it fixes errors in a text so the words say what they were meant to say.
You repair a roof, but you emend a hymnal, a caption, or a proof; the word almost never leaves the world of writing.
Emend belongs to editors, archivists, and anyone correcting a written text; outside writing, plain fix or correct is the natural choice.

Keep it apart from its sound-alike cousin amend, which you met earlier in this course: laws, rules, and plans are amended — improved by change; manuscripts and misprints are emended — restored to what they should have said.

The county historical society owns the only transcript of Mayor Ellison's 1911 flood speech, typed that night by an exhausted clerk.
For a century, visitors read that the mayor had promised 'no new levy' -- a strange vow for a town underwater.
Last spring an archivist located the clerk's shorthand pad and used it to emend the transcript: the mayor had actually promised 'a new levee'.
The society altered nothing else on the page: the job was not to polish the clerk's prose but to restore what the mayor had actually said.
A framed note beside the display now explains the change, so no visitor mistakes the repair for a rewrite.
